title: Dishoom, Gymkhana, and the British Indian Invasion: London's Best Are Finally Coming to America
excerpt: Backed by a $400 million valuation and a sold-out New York pop-up, some of Britain's most celebrated Indian restaurants are crossing the Atlantic — and the diaspora is watching closely.
body:
For decades, the finest Indian restaurants in the English-speaking world lived in London. While New York had its curry houses and San Francisco its progressive Indian eateries, the sheer depth and sophistication of Indian dining in the UK — shaped by generations of South Asian immigration — remained unmatched on American soil.

That is about to change. In what Restaurant Business has called "the year of redefining Indian food in America," 2026 is witnessing an unprecedented wave of acclaimed British Indian restaurant brands crossing the Atlantic to set up shop in the United States.

## The Dishoom Effect

Leading the charge is Dishoom, the beloved Bombay-inspired café chain that has become something of a religion in the UK since its founding in London's Covent Garden in 2010. With 12 locations across Britain paying homage to the vanishing Irani cafés of old Bombay, Dishoom has built a cult following around its bacon naan rolls, keema pau, and fragrant biryanis.

Now, after a sold-out breakfast pop-up at Stephen Starr's Pastis in New York in 2024 — which had lines snaking around the block — Dishoom is finalising plans for a permanent New York City restaurant. Private equity firm L Catterton invested in the company last year in a deal that valued Dishoom at nearly $400 million, providing the financial muscle for its American ambitions.

"I was blown away by breakfast at Dishoom," Pastis owner Stephen Starr told Resy. "There's no Indian restaurant that's ever done that, and I still think about it all the time."

CEO Brian Trollip has confirmed the team has also scouted sites in Boston, Chicago, and Washington, DC, suggesting that New York is just the beginning.

## The JKS Advance Guard

Dishoom is not alone. JKS Restaurants, the London hospitality powerhouse behind Michelin-starred Gymkhana, has already made its American entrance. In December, JKS brought Gymkhana — known for its refined Raj-era club aesthetic and game-meat dishes — to the Aria Resort & Casino in Las Vegas. Earlier in 2026, the group opened Ambassadors Clubhouse, a Punjabi-focused concept, at 1245 Broadway in Manhattan's NoMad neighbourhood.

And the pipeline is growing. The New York Times reports that Asma Khan's Darjeeling Express is slated to open following its own sell-out pop-up, while Indian small plates restaurant Kricket is eyeing a 2026 Manhattan launch.

## Why Now — and Why It Matters for NRIs

For Indian Americans who grew up visiting relatives in London and marvelling at the dining scene, this moment feels personal. Many NRIs have for years carried Dishoom's cookbook home, packed their suitcases with the chain's chai blends, and wondered why nothing comparable existed stateside.

The answer has partly been economic. The UK's Indian dining culture was built on a century of post-colonial immigration; the American market, by contrast, was long dominated by the all-you-can-eat lunch buffet model. But consumer palates have shifted. Indian food is now the fastest-growing global cuisine category in US grocery, and James Beard Awards are regularly going to Indian chefs and restaurants.

The British invasion represents something else, too: validation. When a brand valued at $400 million bets its international expansion on the American appetite for Indian food, it signals that Indian cuisine has arrived not as exotic novelty but as mainstream dining culture.

## What's Next

Dishoom's New York address and opening date remain under wraps, but industry insiders expect doors to open in late 2026 or early 2027. JKS is reportedly evaluating additional US cities. For the diaspora, the question is no longer whether London-quality Indian dining will reach America — it is how fast it will scale once it does.

As Dishoom co-founder Kavi Thakrar put it: "People love our breakfast. We wanted to make sure we could deliver something fantastic." If the Pastis pop-up was any indication, America is more than ready.
